Paper_name: A multi-faceted approach to the study of the relationship between self-esteem and the self-prioritization effect
Summary: A longitudinal study (three sessions, about one week apart) examining the relationship between self-esteem and the self-prioritization effect (SPE) in a sample of Italian undergraduate psychology students from the University of Padova. Session 1 assessed implicit self-esteem (SE-IAT, Name Letter Test) and explicit self-esteem (RSES); Session 2 repeated the SE measures and added the shape-label matching task; Session 3 administered the matching task only (maintaining the shape-identity associations learned at Session 2). The study found a robust SPE at both measurement sessions (faster RTs and higher accuracy for self-matching than stranger-matching trials), with moderate temporal stability of the SPE across sessions, and examined the associations between implicit/explicit self-esteem and the SPE.
Author: Lorenzo Atzeni, Luigi Castelli, Giovanni Galfano, Barbara Penolazzi
Conclusion: The results confirmed a robust self-prioritization effect at both measurement sessions, with participants showing substantially faster RTs and higher accuracy for self-matching trials compared with stranger-matching trials; the SPE demonstrated moderate temporal stability across sessions, aligning with RT-based SPE measures using the stranger baseline. The pattern of associations between self-esteem measures and the SPE is consistent with theoretical accounts of the SPE as a low-level, perceptually driven process (or selectively associated with explicit self-esteem), informing the debate on whether higher-order self-evaluative processes modulate the effect.
